text: Each AI token starts with a row of numbers, called an embedding.
As a neural network processes your message, its layers actively change those numbers to
reflect the surrounding context.
But those new numbers might not match the starting numbers for any token.
How can they still represent meaning?
An exact match isn't necessary.
The relationships between the numbers matter, too.
We can picture those relationships as positions on a map, where nearby positions can represent
similar meanings.
That's the idea behind vector space.
To understand how this works, we can look at a standard geographic map.
A map uses two numbers, latitude and longitude, to describe a physical position.
Dallas, Texas, for example, sits roughly at 33 degrees north, 93 degrees west.
This map shows three cities.
When we add New York City and Mountain View, California, you can see they use those exact
same two dimensions for their coordinates.
On this grid, these two numbers alone provide each city with a defined, fixed position in space.
Let's introduce two new coordinates, 38 degrees north, 120 west, and 40 north, 76 west.
Neither perfectly matches our existing cities, but by measuring physical distance on the
grid, we determine the closest match.
The first lands near Mountain View, the second near New York City.
Distance finds the closest match.
We can apply this mapping logic to objects with more properties.
Instead of two coordinates, Coke, Pepsi, and coffee are described by seven characteristics.
Looking across the rows, the two sodas profiles are nearly identical.
Coffee's numbers differ widely.
These seven ratings give each drink a position in vector space.
This diagram plots our seven-dimensional vectors onto a visual map.
Coke and Pepsi sit tightly together in a soft drinks neighborhood.
Coffee sits isolated.
The physical gap between the sodas is short because their numbers are similar.
The lines out to coffee are long, reflecting a massive numerical difference.
Introduce a mystery drink with a new vector.
Which known drink is it closest to?
It maps right next to Pepsi.
We prove this mathematically.
The first six dimensions match perfectly.
Only the citrus score differs, creating a gap of just 0.1.
Smaller gaps mean closer positions.
AI uses this exact mechanism, but scaled up to thousands of dimensions.
Take the test sentence.
The cat sat on the mat during the May rainstorm because it was tired.
The word it is entirely ambiguous on its own.
On this physical map, the blue it marker starts outside the neighborhoods with its initial numbers.
As layers process the sentence, they mathematically update its numbers with context,
connecting it to cat.
This physically moves the marker across vector space until it lands next to cat.
Meaning is a position in vector space.
Similar meanings usually sit close together.
